slides.title: Direct applicability vs direct effect
slides.text: The 'common mistake' slide again, repeated from the previous lecture as revision.

slides.title: The rule stays the rule
slides.text: Marshall I, Faccini Dori, Delena Wells — no horizontal direct effect of directives.

slides.title: Why not
slides.text: Addressed only to member states; no wrongdoing by the individual; it would erode the regulation/directive distinction; legal certainty.

slides.title: The five workarounds
slides.text: The list again, now worked through one by one over the following slides.

slides.title: Workaround 1: what counts as the state
slides.text: Foster (C-188/89) stretches the vertical route by stretching the defendant. WHO: entities controlled by the state — public undertakings, universities, undertakings with special rights. WHY: because they exercise de facto regulatory power, or provide a public service under state control with special powers. The practical consequence for a case: before concluding that a defendant is 'private', check whether it is an emanation of the state.

terms.def: A body under state control or with special powers beyond those of private parties, against which a directive can be invoked vertically (Foster).

cards.q: A claimant wants to rely on a directive against a state-owned utility with statutory monopoly powers. Vertical or horizontal?
cards.a: Vertical. Under Foster (C-188/89) a body controlled by the state or endowed with special powers beyond those of private parties is an emanation of the state, so the directive can be invoked against it.

slides.title: Workaround 2: indirect effect
slides.text: The duty of national courts to interpret national law, AS FAR AS POSSIBLE, in line with EU law — Von Colson (14/83). Two bases: Article 4(3) TEU, under which member states take any appropriate measure to ensure fulfilment of obligations arising from the Treaties or the acts of the institutions, and effet utile. And the crucial scope note on the slide: this applies to ALL EU LAW, not only to directives.

terms.def: The duty to read national law, so far as possible, in conformity with EU law (Von Colson).

cards.q: What is the legal basis of the duty of consistent interpretation?
cards.a: Article 4(3) TEU — the duty of sincere cooperation to take any appropriate measure to ensure fulfilment of EU obligations — together with effet utile (Von Colson, 14/83).

slides.title: Indirect effect works horizontally
slides.text: Two cases mark the two directions. Von Colson (14/83) is the vertical case; MARLEASING (C-106/89) extends the duty to disputes between private parties. That is why indirect effect matters so much: it reaches where direct effect cannot, and a court in a purely private dispute must still read national law in conformity with the directive.

cards.q: Does the duty of consistent interpretation apply in a dispute between two private parties?
cards.a: Yes — Marleasing (C-106/89). This is what makes indirect effect the principal workaround around the absence of horizontal direct effect.

slides.title: The scope of indirect effect
slides.text: Broad on every axis. It binds ANY state authority — courts and administration alike. It covers ALL national law, whether adopted to transpose the directive or enacted BEFORE it (Marleasing). The transposition period must generally have expired, but even before expiry courts must refrain from interpretations liable to compromise the directive's result (Adeneler, C-212/04). And the decisive advantage over direct effect: the directive's provisions do NOT have to be clear, precise and unconditional.

cards.q: Name two ways in which indirect effect is broader than direct effect.
cards.a: It operates horizontally as well as vertically, and the directive's provisions need not be clear, precise and unconditional. It also covers all national law, including law predating the directive.

slides.title: The limits of indirect effect
slides.text: Two. No CONTRA LEGEM interpretation — the court cannot read national law against its clear wording, though the qualification 'as far as possible' is generous and Quelle (C-404/06) shows how far the Court will push it. And it cannot impose or aggravate CRIMINAL LIABILITY on an individual (Pupino, C-105/03). Note the symmetry with direct effect: both doctrines stop at the criminal law.

terms.def: Against the clear wording of the national provision; the outer limit of consistent interpretation.

cards.q: What are the two limits of the duty of consistent interpretation?
cards.a: It cannot go contra legem — against the clear wording of national law — and it cannot impose or aggravate criminal liability on an individual (Pupino, C-105/03).

slides.title: Where the boundary blurs
slides.text: Pfeiffer (C-397-403/01) and Océano Grupo (C-240/98) are the cases where consistent interpretation does so much work that it becomes hard to distinguish from horizontal direct effect. The formal rule is intact — the court is applying national law, interpreted in conformity — but the practical result for the private defendant is the same. Worth a sentence in an essay on whether the rule against horizontal direct effect still means anything.

slides.title: Workaround 3: triangular situations
slides.text: Delena Wells (C-201/02): an individual invokes a directive VERTICALLY against the state, and the consequence of the state complying is adverse for another private party. That is permitted — the adverse effect on the third party is an incidental consequence, not the direct imposition of an obligation on them by the directive.

terms.def: Adverse repercussions for a private third party flowing from a directive invoked against the state; permissible.

cards.q: A neighbour invokes an environmental directive against the authority that granted a company its permit. May the court apply the directive even though the company loses out?
cards.a: Yes. That is a triangular situation (Delena Wells, C-201/02): the directive is invoked vertically against the state, and adverse consequences for the third party are merely incidental, not a horizontal obligation.

slides.title: The technical standards line
slides.text: The classic field for incidental effect is the directive on notification of technical standards: CIA Security (C-194/94) and Unilever (C-443/98). A national technical rule adopted without the required notification cannot be applied — even in a dispute between two private parties, because the defect is a procedural one in the national rule rather than an obligation imposed by the directive on the individual.

cards.q: Why can an unnotified national technical standard be set aside even in a private dispute?
cards.a: Because the directive imposes a procedural notification duty on the STATE; its breach makes the national rule inapplicable. No obligation is imposed on the private party by the directive (CIA Security, Unilever).

slides.title: Workaround 4: directives expressing general principles
slides.text: Mangold (C-144/04) and Kücükdeveci (C-555/07). A directive can give expression to a general principle of EU law — non-discrimination on grounds of age being the example — and general principles are directly applicable because they have their basis in PRIMARY law. So the rule against horizontal direct effect of directives is bypassed: what applies horizontally is the principle, with the directive giving it concrete shape.

cards.q: How did Mangold and Kücükdeveci get around the absence of horizontal direct effect?
cards.a: By locating the operative rule in a general principle of EU law — non-discrimination on grounds of age — which has its basis in primary law and is therefore directly applicable horizontally; the directive merely gives it concrete expression.

slides.title: A newer route: the Charter
slides.text: Case C-715/20, KL: the right to an effective remedy in Article 47 of the Charter may be invoked IN CONJUNCTION WITH Directive 1999/70 in a dispute between private individuals. The technique is the same as Mangold — a primary-law provision does the horizontal work — but the vehicle is now a Charter right. Watch this line; it is where the doctrine is currently moving.

cards.q: Can a Charter right be invoked together with a directive in a purely private dispute?
cards.a: Yes, on the C-715/20 KL line: Article 47 of the Charter may be invoked in conjunction with a directive between private individuals, because the operative norm is primary law.

slides.title: Workaround 5: conditional benefits under a regulation
slides.text: Viamex Agrar (C-37 and 58/06). Directives cannot have horizontal direct effect — but they may in effect do so where benefits under a REGULATION are made conditional on compliance with a directive. The regulation supplies the horizontal force; the directive supplies the condition.

slides.title: Critical literature
slides.text: A slide of academic criticism of the doctrine.

slides.title: Newest developments
slides.text: Gabel Industria Tessile (C-316/22), with Thelen Technopark (C-261/20) alongside. Two points. Horizontal direct effect may be produced by NATIONAL law itself. And a lesson about the interaction of direct effect, procedural autonomy and effectiveness: where national law provides that unduly paid taxes passed on to a consumer can be recovered only in a civil action against the supplier, who may then claim from the state, and recovery from the supplier is barred by the prohibition of horizontal direct effect, then claiming directly from the STATE must be available — otherwise the right would be practically impossible to exercise.

cards.q: What does Gabel Industria Tessile (C-316/22) show about the interaction of horizontal direct effect and effectiveness?
cards.a: That where the prohibition of horizontal direct effect blocks the only national route to recovery, effectiveness requires an alternative — here, a direct claim against the state.

slides.title: The three-step approach
slides.text: The schema again: conditions, category, relationship.

slides.title: Direct effect and decentralised enforcement
slides.text: The pairing that structures this part: EU law confers rights, and those rights are enforced through national machinery.

slides.title: Decentralised enforcement as the rule
slides.text: Member states are generally responsible for enforcing and implementing EU acts — through their AUTHORITIES under Article 291(1) TFEU and through their COURTS under Article 19(1) second subparagraph TEU. Direct enforcement by the Union itself is the exception and requires an EXPLICIT legal rule. Structurally this is the opposite of a federal state: the Union legislates, the member states administer.

cards.q: Who enforces EU law, and what are the Treaty bases?
cards.a: The member states as a rule — their authorities under Article 291(1) TFEU and their courts under Article 19(1) second subparagraph TEU. Direct Union enforcement exists only where an explicit rule provides for it.

slides.title: Where the Union enforces directly
slides.text: Competition law and the Digital Markets Act; foreign trade law; Union funds; research and science funding; and cross-sectional tasks such as human resources, budget and internal organisation.

cards.q: Give examples of areas where the Union enforces EU law directly rather than through the member states.
cards.a: Competition law and the DMA, foreign trade law, Union funds, research and science funding, and the Union's own internal administration.

slides.title: The structure of decentralised enforcement
slides.text: Three layers, drawn as a pyramid: EU procedural rules at the top; below them procedural autonomy; and framing that autonomy, the principles of equivalence and effectiveness — Rewe (33/76) and Comet (45/76).

slides.title: Rewe: the starting point
slides.text: The prohibitions at issue had direct effect and conferred rights on citizens which national courts are required to protect. The question was then how those rights are to be pursued.

slides.title: Rewe: procedural autonomy
slides.text: In the ABSENCE of Union rules on the subject, it is for the domestic legal system of each member state to designate the courts having jurisdiction and to determine the procedural conditions governing actions intended to protect the rights individuals derive from the direct effect of Union law.

slides.title: Rewe: the two limits
slides.text: EQUIVALENCE: those conditions cannot be LESS FAVOURABLE than those relating to similar actions of a domestic nature. EFFECTIVENESS: the position would be different only if the conditions and time-limits made it IMPOSSIBLE IN PRACTICE to exercise rights which national courts are obliged to protect. Note the original wording — 'impossible in practice' — which the later formula softens.

slides.title: The modern formula
slides.text: From Impact (C-268/06), and worth learning verbatim because it is the sentence to quote: in the absence of Union rules it is for the domestic legal system to designate the courts and lay down the detailed procedural rules governing actions safeguarding rights individuals derive from Union law; those rules must be NO LESS FAVOURABLE than those governing similar domestic actions (equivalence) and must not render PRACTICALLY IMPOSSIBLE OR EXCESSIVELY DIFFICULT the exercise of rights conferred by Union law (effectiveness). Note the softening: 'excessively difficult' is a lower bar than Rewe's 'impossible in practice'.

cards.q: State the equivalence and effectiveness principles in their modern formulation.
cards.a: National procedural rules must be no less favourable than those governing similar domestic actions (equivalence), and must not render practically impossible or excessively difficult the exercise of rights conferred by EU law (effectiveness) — Impact, C-268/06.

slides.title: Where the EU has its own procedural rules
slides.text: They take precedence over national rules. Examples: Articles 77 ff. GDPR, and the Antitrust Damages Directive 2014/104/EU. So the first question is always whether EU procedural rules exist — procedural autonomy is only the residual answer.

cards.q: In what order do you analyse the procedural framework for enforcing an EU right?
cards.a: First ask whether EU procedural rules exist (e.g. GDPR Arts 77 ff., the Antitrust Damages Directive) — they take precedence. Only in their absence does national procedural autonomy apply, framed by equivalence and effectiveness.

slides.title: Procedural autonomy
slides.text: Where there are no EU rules, it is for the national legal order to enforce EU law through its general rules and procedures.

slides.title: The two principles as minimum standards
slides.text: Equivalence and effectiveness are minimum quality standards on national procedure, grounded in the principle of sincere cooperation and loyalty in Article 4(3) TEU and in the right to an effective remedy in Article 19(1) TEU.

slides.title: Equivalence, defined
slides.text: National procedural rules for actions safeguarding EU rights must not be less favourable than those governing similar domestic actions — in substance a non-discrimination rule, comparing the EU claim with its closest domestic analogue.

slides.title: Effectiveness, defined
slides.text: National procedural rules must not render the exercise of EU rights practically impossible or excessively difficult. Unlike equivalence, this is an absolute standard: it does not matter that domestic claims are treated just as badly.

cards.q: A national time-limit of two weeks applies equally to EU-based and domestic claims. Can it still breach EU law?
cards.a: Yes. Equivalence is satisfied, but effectiveness is an independent, absolute standard: if the limit renders the exercise of the EU right practically impossible or excessively difficult, it must be set aside.

slides.title: What follows from a breach
slides.text: A three-step remedy: first interpret the national rule in conformity with EU law; if that is impossible, disapply it in line with primacy; and — a question mark on the slide — possibly base a remedy directly on Article 4(3) TEU.

slides.title: Res judicata: Kühne & Heitz
slides.text: How far effectiveness reaches into final decisions. C-453/00: the duty of cooperation in Article 4(3) TEU obliges an administrative body to REVIEW a final administrative decision, on application, to take account of an interpretation the Court has given in the meantime — but only where four conditions are met: national law gives it the power to reopen; the decision became final through a judgment of a court ruling at final instance; that judgment rested on a misinterpretation of EU law adopted WITHOUT a preliminary reference; and the person complained to the authority immediately after learning of the Court's decision. Four cumulative conditions, which is why the case rarely helps in practice.

cards.q: Under what conditions must a final administrative decision be reviewed in the light of later CJEU case law?
cards.a: Kühne & Heitz: national law allows reopening; the decision became final through a judgment at final instance; that judgment misinterpreted EU law without making a preliminary reference; and the person complained immediately after learning of the Court's ruling. All four cumulatively.

slides.title: Francovich: the facts
slides.text: Italy failed to implement a directive requiring a guarantee system for unpaid wages in the event of the employer's bankruptcy. Francovich and Bonifaci, employees of a bankrupt company, did not receive what they were owed. The Court held that the directive's provisions LACKED SUFFICIENT PRECISION to be directly effective — there was no way to know who should pay — but that they clearly intended to confer rights of which the individuals had been deprived by the state's failure. Hence the question: can they claim damages against Italy?

slides.title: Francovich: the new legal order argument
slides.text: The Court repeats the Van Gend en Loos passage — the Treaty created its own legal system whose subjects include nationals, conferring rights that become part of their legal patrimony.

slides.title: Francovich: the effectiveness argument
slides.text: The FULL EFFECTIVENESS of Union rules would be impaired and the protection of the rights they grant weakened if individuals were unable to obtain redress when their rights are infringed by a breach of Union law for which a member state can be held responsible.

slides.title: Francovich: the holding
slides.text: The principle that a state must be liable for loss and damage caused to individuals by breaches of Union law for which it can be held responsible is INHERENT IN THE SYSTEM OF THE TREATY. Developed further in Brasserie du Pêcheur (C-46/93 and C-48/93).

cards.q: Why did Francovich need state liability rather than direct effect?
cards.a: Because the directive's provisions lacked sufficient precision to be directly effective — they did not identify who was to pay — yet clearly intended to confer rights. Liability in damages was the only remaining protection.

slides.title: The reason
slides.text: The full effectiveness of EU law — effet utile — in a functionality approach. The same argument that produced direct effect produces liability when direct effect is unavailable.

slides.title: The legal basis
slides.text: A GENERAL PRINCIPLE of EU law, derived inter alia from Articles 4(3) and 19(1) TEU and from effet utile. The slide is emphatic about what it is NOT: not Article 340 TFEU, which governs the liability of the UNION; and not member state law, although member state law supplies the procedure. Getting this right is worth a mark.

cards.q: What is the legal basis of member state liability for breaches of EU law?
cards.a: A general principle of EU law derived from Arts 4(3) and 19(1) TEU and effet utile — NOT Article 340 TFEU, which concerns the liability of the Union, and not national law, which only supplies the procedure.

slides.title: The conditions of state liability
slides.text: Five, and they must be recited in order. A BREACH of EU law by the member state, by act or omission. The breached provision must be INTENDED TO CONFER RIGHTS on individuals. The breach must be SUFFICIENTLY QUALIFIED AND SERIOUS. There must be DAMAGE. And a CAUSAL LINK between breach and damage. The third is where most cases are decided: a total failure to transpose a directive is automatically sufficiently serious, while a defensible misreading of an unclear provision is usually not.

terms.def: A manifest and grave disregard of the limits on a state's discretion; non-transposition of a directive is automatically sufficiently serious.

cards.q: State the conditions for member state liability in damages under EU law.
cards.a: A breach by act or omission; the breached rule intended to confer rights on individuals; the breach sufficiently serious; damage; and a causal link between the breach and the damage.

cards.q: A member state fails to transpose a directive at all. Is the breach sufficiently serious?
cards.a: Yes — complete failure to transpose within the deadline is per se a sufficiently serious breach, because the state had no discretion to exercise.

slides.title: Which organ's breach counts
slides.text: All three. The LEGISLATURE, as in Francovich. The ADMINISTRATION — Danske Slagterier (C-445/06). And the JUDICIARY — Köbler (C-224/01), where a supreme court's manifest misapplication of EU law, including a failure to refer, can engage the state's liability. Köbler is the striking one, since it means a final judgment can found a damages claim against the same state whose courts gave it.

cards.q: Can a member state be liable in damages for a judgment of its own supreme court?
cards.a: Yes — Köbler (C-224/01). Liability covers breaches by the legislature, the administration and the judiciary, though for a final-instance court the breach must be a manifest infringement.

slides.title: Who enforces it
slides.text: The member states, under procedural autonomy framed by equivalence and effectiveness — so the claim is brought in the national courts, under national procedural rules, with the EU conditions supplying the substance.

cards.q: Where does an individual bring a Francovich claim?
cards.a: Before the national courts, under national procedural rules — procedural autonomy limited by equivalence and effectiveness. EU law supplies the conditions of liability, national law the procedure.

slides.title: From state liability to tortious liability
slides.text: The step from the vertical relationship to the horizontal one: if the state must pay for breaching EU law, what about a private party that does?

slides.title: Courage and Manfredi
slides.text: Courage (C-453/99) and Manfredi (C-295-298/04): the full effectiveness of the competition prohibition would be put at risk if it were not open to ANY INDIVIDUAL to claim damages for loss caused by a contract or conduct liable to restrict or distort competition. The same effet utile reasoning as Francovich, now producing a private damages claim between individuals — and later codified in the Antitrust Damages Directive.

cards.q: On what reasoning did the Court create a private right to damages for breach of EU competition law?
cards.a: Effet utile: the full effectiveness of the prohibition would be at risk if any individual could not claim damages for loss caused by anti-competitive conduct (Courage C-453/99, Manfredi C-295-298/04).
